chapter: Paris scene and a visit home, 1937-39
title: Oscar Ellman, the Argentine guitarist
summary: Ellman was a complete guitarist, aspiring to Segovia's mastery yet able to play jazz, whose stinging notes contrasted with Django's, and who jammed with Bernard Addison.

story.theme_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section: instruments and players
story.community_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section's changing role

blocks.x: Before you say that, I was wondering could you elaborate a little bit more about this guitarist from the Argentine?

Oh, Oscar Edmund, Ellman, he was complete. He played 'Flamingo', he played, he was complete guitarist complete. Melody all, it was complete. Like the master, what did master in Spanish m_an? He was his goal was to be like Segovia (unintelligible) I believe but he could play jazz.

You see, Tango could play, could find those beautiful notes. He could find them, see? He would get one of his notes would be three or four of another man's notes. But Oscar, his note was stinging you. He was just
in there. That was it. But it wasn't a thing of battering each other, they just played and laughed and drink cognac and go home.
Well, I was just wondering if you hear more about him because I hadn't heard.
Oh, yes. One of our great guitarists, Bernard Addison. They were jamming, but I was surprised. He was surprised, and that's what happened.
